name: Belgium

findings.summary: Proximus and Orange Belgium chose Nokia to renew their shared radio access network across 2G-5G, with Ericsson supplying the 5G core; the overhaul was due to finish by 2023.
findings.analyst_inference: Nokia (Finnish) and Ericsson (Swedish) are both third-pole vendors. Proximus said the tender would save about EUR80m capex over 2021-23 versus plan; contract value undisclosed. Completion of the 2023 overhaul was not confirmed in this pass, so still_current is null.

findings.reversal_of: Huawei single-RAN (2G/3G/4G) at Proximus and Orange Belgium
findings.summary: Both leading Belgian operators are removing Huawei, their sole radio-network supplier (Proximus since 2009), replacing it with Nokia so the networks would be free of Chinese equipment by 2023.
findings.analyst_inference: Reversal of an operational (tier 5) Huawei single-RAN at both operators. Operators cited technical, operational and financial criteria and Huawei called it a free-market tender, but the swap followed the June 2020 high-risk-vendor decision (BEL-003) and Orange's former CEO cited the risk of a network being stopped; coded geopolitical, though commercial is arguable. Completion not confirmed.

findings.reversal_of: High-risk vendors' (Huawei) eligibility for Belgian 5G core and >35% of RAN
findings.summary: Belgium's National Security Council barred high-risk suppliers from 5G core networks, capped them at 35% of non-core network parts and kept them out of sensitive areas such as near military sites, while declining an outright Huawei ban.
findings.analyst_inference: An exclusion, so coded as a reversal of Huawei's eligibility. Huawei held no 5G core role (Ericsson supplied core), so tier 3 is a conservative stand-in rather than the tier of an installed system; the operators' tier-5 RAN swap is BEL-002. BIPT opened page gives only the NSC approval date; content from Brussels Times and Light Reading (citing Politico). A law of 17 Feb 2022 created a ministerial 5G authorisation regime (Stibbe), but whether high-risk-vendor rules were codified was not confirmed.

findings.summary: Google's Saint-Ghislain data-centre campus in Hainaut is operating with about 600 staff; Google reports over EUR11bn invested there since 2007 and lists it among its Google Cloud locations.
findings.analyst_inference: Owner-operator is Google (US). The EUR11bn cumulative figure is from VRT and is not converted or coded as a value. Date is the status observation date, not the opening date.

findings.summary: Google announced a new EUR5bn investment over 2026-27 to expand its Saint-Ghislain campus for AI and Google Cloud, adding 300 full-time jobs.
findings.analyst_inference: Coded tier 1: an announced investment programme; no construction start or permit was confirmed. EUR5bn is about US$5.8bn at Oct 2025 rates, but the value field is left null because the conversion rate on the source date was not checked in this pass.

findings.summary: Google signed new carbon-free energy deals with Eneco, Luminus and Renner totalling over 110 MW for its Belgian operations, and says it has supported 365 MW of new clean energy in Belgium overall.
findings.analyst_inference: Pole null: the plants are controlled by several developers (Eneco and Luminus have foreign parents; Renner's ownership not checked), and Google is only the offtaker. Tier 3 assumes the deals are signed PPAs; terms and values were not disclosed.

findings.controller: EuroHPC Joint Undertaking (LUMI and JUPITER AI Factories)
findings.summary: EuroHPC selected Belgium's AI Factory Antenna (BE-AIFA), a EUR10m imec-coordinated hub linking Belgian users to the LUMI (Finland) and JUPITER (Germany) AI supercomputers; full services expected by September 2026.
findings.analyst_inference: Compute is controlled by EU-level EuroHPC and hosted in Finland and Germany, so third pole; Belgium hosts no AI Factory itself. Tier 3 as a binding EU selection with co-funding; EUR10m budget not converted. Underlying GPU vendors not stated in sources.

findings.base_model: Mistral AI models (Le Chat, Mistral Code)
findings.summary: Proximus NXT partnered with Mistral AI to offer Le Chat, AI Studio and Mistral Code as a managed, Proximus-hosted service for organisations in the Benelux and wider Europe.
findings.analyst_inference: Mistral (French) supplies and updates the models, so third pole even though Proximus hosts. Coded tier 2 as a commercial partnership with no named customers or value; not government adoption.

findings.summary: Belgium's defence minister told parliament that about 30 Hikvision and Dahua surveillance cameras used by Defence posed limited espionage risk because they were not internet-connected.
findings.analyst_inference: Small deployment inside a national ministry; scale coded municipal for its size. Single opened S3 source; whether the cameras remain in use was not checked.

findings.summary: After a December 2021 cyberattack, Belgian Defence bought hundreds of Huawei wifi routers for a temporary internet-research network; military intelligence said it carried no sensitive data and parliamentarians demanded a correction.
findings.analyst_inference: Small, temporary procurement; scale coded municipal for size. No replacement decision was reported in the source; whether the routers were withdrawn was not checked.

silicon.null_reason: no Belgian accelerator purchase or export-licence evidence surfaced; one Proximus/Mistral/Nvidia search returned none, and BE-AIFA sources name no GPU vendor

research_gaps: Did Proximus and Orange Belgium complete the Huawei-to-Nokia RAN swap by 2023, and does Huawei retain any role?
Telenet/Wyre (Liberty Global) and DIGI Belgium RAN and core vendors were not found; one search returned only Norwegian results.
Were the June 2020 National Security Council high-risk-vendor rules (core exclusion, 35% cap) codified in the 17 Feb 2022 law or a royal decree, and is a high-risk vendor list in force?
Google Saint-Ghislain: has the EUR5bn 2026-27 expansion started construction, and which accelerators (TPU/Nvidia) are deployed?
Other large Belgian data-centre projects since 2023 (e.g. Microsoft Belgium Central region facilities, AWS sovereign Local Zone) and their controllers.
Were Defence's Huawei routers and Hikvision/Dahua cameras removed, and is there any federal rule on Chinese cameras?
Any Belgian sovereign LLM or government adoption of a frontier model provider beyond the DeepSeek device ban already in the global layer.
